obsession: Does the feed run on the same handkerchief - is the attention economy the conjurer's trick that makes the authentic and the artificial interchangeable and profitable, the white-rabbit mechanism that re-extracts the menace (the real crisis) as content (the engagement) when the audience is ready for the sequel? (q0097)
book: Information Doesn't Want to Be Free (Cory Doctorow, 2014)
collision: The same per-person ledger, inverted: c01933 - the lock-holder hoards the per-person stream accounting as a lump (Merlin's guarantee = six times the royalties, the labels keep it) vs c01946 - the Humble Bundle shows the donor the same accounting ('Windows users are giving an average of $40') and the fan pays more from competitive shame. The ledger is the handkerchief's engine: hoarded, it owns the audience; shown, it taxes the fan.
mutation_note: The book finishes at the ceiling with the trick's answer to scarcity named as a change of species - the dandelion (seeds to the wind, no mourning) - and the direct wire's last node revealed as its own lock (PayPal freezes the account). The abundance economy does not end the lock, it reclassifies it: the seeds are the fans, and the fans pay more because they can see what the other fans pay.

fragments.text: Digital locks turn paying customers into pirates... Locking users out doesn't reduce downloads, it reduces sales. (p.59)
fragments.collision: Apple is the lock's most aggressive enforcer (c01903, p.38-40), yet the lock's own store converts its paying customers into pirates (c01926, p.58-59) — the enforcer's refusal to sell is the lock's commercial function

fragments.source: Information Doesn't Want to Be Free (Cory Doctorow, 2014)
fragments.text: The more famous—the more copied—Randall's comics get, the more money he makes. He doesn't need to control or reduce copies. Good thing, because he knows he can't. (p.84)
fragments.collision: The copy IS the marketing engine: the more copied Randall's comics get, the more he earns (c01937, p.84) — yet the lock, the only tool for controlling copies, is aimed at that very copy; and the RIAA's piracy math (c01941, p.84) prices the download as a lost album the buyer never wanted. The enforcer's tool targets the asset the artist profits from
